status: Drafted from a direct, full read of the real Geneva Bible 1560 extracted text (all 16 chapters, 339 verses) — single-pass hand draft grounded in the actual narrative, not yet run through a separate adversarial fact-check pass (this book does not exist in the KJV Character Index, so there was no prior baseline to cross-check against). Ready for a corrective/verification pass on the same schedule as other freshly-drafted books.

characters.name: Nebuchadnezzar

verses.note: Introduced as king reigning over the Assyrians in Nineveh, in the twelfth year of his reign.
Makes war against king Arphaxad of the Medes in the great plain near Ragau.
Swears by his own throne and kingdom to avenge himself on Cilicia, Damascus, Syria, Moab, Ammon, Judaea and Egypt after the western nations refuse to send him aid.
Personally defeats and kills Arphaxad in the mountains of Ragau, taking Ecbatana.
Summons Holofernes and commissions him with a huge army to execute the vengeance decreed in council, demanding total submission ('earth and water') from the west.
Quoted by Holofernes as declaring himself effectively a god ('who is God but Nebuchadnezzar?') whose word cannot fail.
Referred to throughout Holofernes' and Judith's speeches as 'king of all the earth' whose power all creatures are said to serve.

funFacts: Real, well-attested textual feature (not an extraction artifact): this book calls him king of the Assyrians ruling from Nineveh — historically Nebuchadnezzar II was a Neo-Babylonian king, and the Assyrian capital Nineveh had already fallen roughly a decade before his reign began. Judith is widely read as a theological/didactic narrative rather than strict history, and this anachronism is part of the book's own text, preserved as-is rather than corrected.

characters.name: Arphaxad

verses.note: King of the Medes at Ecbatana; builds massive fortified walls and towers around his capital.
Defeated in battle by Nebuchadnezzar in the seventeenth year, hunted into the mountains of Ragau, and killed there.

funFacts: NAMING COLLISION, flagged not merged: this Arphaxad, a king of the Medes, is a completely different figure from Arphaxad son of Shem in Genesis 10:22-24/11:10-13, a post-Flood patriarch. Same name, unrelated person, no textual link between them.

characters.name: Holofernes

verses.note: Named chief captain of Nebuchadnezzar's host, next in rank after the king himself.
Leads the army through the coastlands, receiving submission from Sidon, Tyre and neighboring cities, then encamps to gather baggage before advancing on Judaea.
Rages at Achior's warning speech, declares Nebuchadnezzar the only god, and has Achior bound and delivered to Bethulia to die with the Israelites.
Moves the full army against Bethulia and besieges it, cutting off the water supply.
Receives Judith into his tent, marvels at her beauty and wisdom, and is deceived by her false promise to deliver Israel to him.
Holds a private feast and, through his eunuch Bagoas, has Judith brought in, growing enamored and drinking more wine than ever before in his life.
Passes out drunk alone with Judith in his tent; she beheads him with his own scimitar.
His severed head is displayed by Judith as proof of the Lord's deliverance, and later hung on Bethulia's wall (14:1,11).

funFacts: The 'canopy' woven with purple, gold, emeralds and precious stones over his bed (10:21) recurs as a trophy motif — Judith takes it down before fleeing (13:9) and later dedicates it to the Lord in Jerusalem (16:19).

verses.note: The eunuch in charge of all Holofernes' affairs; sent to persuade Judith to join the feast, framing her refusal as a shame to his master.
Goes to wake Holofernes the next morning, finds him dead and beheaded on the threshold, and raises the alarm with loud weeping and torn garments.
Introduced as leader of all the children of Ammon, in Holofernes' war council.
Recounts Israel's history (Chaldean origins, Egypt, the Exodus, conquest of Canaan) and warns Holofernes that Israel cannot be beaten while faithful to their God.
Holofernes scorns him as a hireling of Ammon and Ephraim and condemns him to die alongside Israel.
Bound and cast out at the foot of the hill beneath Bethulia by Holofernes' soldiers.
Rescued by the men of Bethulia, brought before the rulers, retells Holofernes' words, and is comforted and feasted by Ozias.
Summoned to view Holofernes' severed head; falls on his face and faints, then recovers and does reverence to Judith.
Believes in the God of Israel exceedingly upon seeing what has happened, is circumcised, and is joined to the house of Israel from that day.

characters.name: Ozias

verses.note: Named as one of three rulers of Bethulia (with Chabris and Charmis) who receive the rescued Achior.
Confronted by the desperate, thirst-stricken people demanding surrender; persuades them to hold out five more days for the Lord's mercy, promising to yield the city if none comes.
Rebuked by Judith for putting God to the test with the five-day oath; humbly accepts her correction, praises her wisdom, and grants her leave to go out from the city with her maid.
Present at the gate with the elders when Judith departs, marveling at her transformed beauty and blessing her purpose.
Blesses Judith before the assembled people as exalted above all women for delivering Israel by her own hand.
Sends word throughout the region to rally Israel's pursuit of the fleeing Assyrian army.

funFacts: NAMING NOTE: 'Ozias' is the Greek/Septuagint-style rendering of the Hebrew name elsewhere Anglicized as 'Uzziah' — this ruler of Bethulia is not the same figure as any King Uzziah of Judah found elsewhere in scripture; flagged so the shared underlying name is not mistaken for identity.

verses.note: One of the three elders of Bethulia who receive Achior, alongside Ozias and Charmis.
Summoned by Judith along with Ozias and Charmis to hear her rebuke of the city's oath.
Present at the city gate to see Judith depart.
One of the three elders of Bethulia who receive Achior, alongside Ozias and Chabris.
Summoned by Judith along with Ozias and Chabris to hear her rebuke of the city's oath.
Present at the city gate to see Judith depart.

characters.name: Joakim

verses.note: The high priest at Jerusalem; writes to Bethulia and Betomesthaim ordering them to seize and hold the mountain passes to block the invasion route into Judaea.
Leads the priests in Jerusalem in wearing sackcloth about their loins, offering the continual burnt offering, and putting ashes on their mitres while crying to the Lord for the whole house of Israel.
Comes with the senate of Israel from Jerusalem after the victory specifically to see Judith and bless her as the exaltation of Jerusalem and glory of Israel.

funFacts: NAMING NOTE: 'Joakim' is a variant spelling of the same underlying name as 'Jehoiakim' (a king of Judah) and other priestly 'Joacims' elsewhere in scripture/tradition — this is specifically the high priest presiding in Jerusalem during the Assyrian invasion in Judith, not any king; flagged given the shared name form.

characters.name: Judith

genealogy.father: Merari (see genealogyLists.judithLineage for her full stated patrilineal chain back to Israel)

verses.note: Introduced with a long stated genealogy back to the patriarch Israel; a wealthy, God-fearing widow of the tribe of Simeon, three years and four months a widow, living in fasting and sackcloth.
Summons Ozias, Chabris and Charmis and rebukes the city's oath to surrender in five days as putting God to the test, urging faith instead.
Announces she will do a deed that will be remembered by all generations, but refuses to reveal her plan in advance.
Prays at length before departing, invoking the vengeance of her ancestor Simeon and asking God to break Assyria's strength by the hand of a woman.
Bathes, anoints herself, and dresses in her finest garments and jewelry to beguile Holofernes' men, then leaves the city with her maid.
Deceives Holofernes with a false prophecy that Israel is about to sin and become vulnerable, promising to lead him to easy victory.
Refuses Holofernes' food and wine, keeping her own kosher provisions, and goes out nightly to the valley to pray and bathe.
Left alone with the drunken Holofernes; takes his own scimitar and beheads him, then places his head in her food bag.
Returns to Bethulia, displays Holofernes' head to the city, and gives God the credit for the killing.
Instructs the men of Bethulia to hang the head on the wall and feign an attack at dawn to rout the leaderless Assyrian camp.
Given Holofernes' tent, silver, and furniture as spoil by the people; celebrated by all the women of Israel with a dance she leads.
Sings a victory hymn to God recounting how a woman's hand, not strength of arms, brought down Assyria's mightiest captain.
Returns to Bethulia, remains unmarried the rest of her life, and dies there at the age of one hundred and five, buried in her husband Manasses' cave.

ageEvents.event: Died at Bethulia, per Judith 16:23; mourned by Israel for seven days.

funFacts: NAMING COLLISION, flagged not merged: this Judith is a completely different person from the Judith of Genesis 26:34 (a Hittite wife of Esau, daughter of Beeri) — same name, no textual connection whatsoever between the two.
Her sandal is singled out poetically in her own victory hymn as part of what disarmed Holofernes: 'Her sandal ravished his eye' (16:9) — the motif behind this tier's name.

verses.note: Judith's husband, of her own tribe and family; dies of heatstroke while overseeing sheaf-binders during barley harvest, and is buried at Bethulia between Dothaim and Balamon.
Left Judith gold, silver, servants, cattle and lands, on which she lived as a wealthy widow.
Judith remains devoted to his memory her whole life and is buried in his own burial cave upon her death.

characters.name: Judith's Handmaid

verses.note: Described as the maid set over all Judith's household affairs, sent to summon the city's elders.
Packs Judith's provisions and accompanies her out of Bethulia toward the Assyrian camp.
Carries and holds the bag into which Judith places Holofernes' severed head, and returns with her to Bethulia.
Freed by Judith near the end of her long life, alongside the distribution of her goods.

funFacts: Never named in the text — kept as an unnamed collective/individual entry per the naming-collision and no-invention rules rather than assigning her a traditional name not present in this translation.

genealogyLists.note: Bulk/unresolved references, kept out of the character list above.

judithLineage.note: Judith's full stated patrilineal chain, given in one verse: daughter of Merari, son of Ox, son of Joseph, son of Oziel, son of Elkiah, son of Ananias, son of Gideon, son of Raphaim, son of Ahitub, son of Elihu, son of Eliab, son of Nathanael, son of Salamiel, son of Salasadai, son of Israel. Only Merari (her direct father) is captured in her genealogy.father field above; the remaining ancestors are logged here in bulk since none of them appear as narrative actors.

bethuliaElders.note: Chabris son of Gothoniel and Charmis son of Melchiel — their fathers Gothoniel and Melchiel are named only as genealogy, with no independent narrative role of their own.

notes: Judith does not exist in the KJV canon or the existing KJV Character Index — it is a deuterocanonical book unique to this Geneva Bible (1560) translation, drafted fresh here. Structurally it is almost entirely narrative/person-driven across all 16 chapters (no thin-content law/theme sections comparable to Leviticus or the Pauline epistles), so every tier is Person-type; even Judith's lengthy prayer (ch.9) and victory hymn (ch.16) stay folded into her own manager tier rather than becoming separate Law tiers, since she personally speaks them as her own act, not received/transmitted instruction. Six major managers cover the book's two parallel threads: the Assyrian chain of command (Nebuchadnezzar, who personally wages the opening war against Arphaxad and commissions the invasion; Holofernes, his field commander and the book's antagonist) and the Israelite response (Achior the Ammonite defector-turned-convert; Ozias, the ruler of Bethulia who nearly surrenders the city; Joakim, the high priest whose Jerusalem thread runs in parallel to the Bethulia siege; and Judith herself, whose assassination of Holofernes resolves both threads at once). Six submanagers attach to their narratively-linked major: Arphaxad under Nebuchadnezzar (his defeated rival, not a self-driving agent in the main plot); Bagoas under Holofernes (his chamberlain, who discovers the body); Chabris and Charmis under Ozias (the two co-elders always named alongside him, never acting independently of him); and Judith's husband Manasses and her unnamed handmaid both under Judith (family/direct-support, loyalty-boost). A real, load-bearing historical inconsistency is preserved rather than corrected: the text itself calls Nebuchadnezzar king of the Assyrians reigning from Nineveh, though historically Nebuchadnezzar II ruled Neo-Babylon and Nineveh had already fallen before his reign — this is a known, deliberate feature of Judith as a theological narrative rather than strict history, not an artifact of the Geneva extraction. Three real naming collisions were caught and flagged rather than merged: this book's Judith is unrelated to the Judith of Genesis 26:34 (Esau's Hittite wife); this book's Arphaxad (a king of the Medes) is unrelated to the patriarch Arphaxad son of Shem in Genesis 10-11; and 'Ozias'/'Joakim' share underlying name-forms with other unrelated figures elsewhere in scripture (Uzziah, Jehoiakim) despite no textual link. Judith's full stated ancestry (Judith 8:1, fifteen generations back to Israel) is logged in genealogyLists rather than individually indexed, matching how Matthew's genealogy was handled in the KJV index, since none of those named ancestors act in the story.
